prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its biologically active form, which made incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: After reading the full first round and my own chair's questions, I keep my configuration unchanged: a single-part B049 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The case is still the science. GLP-1 is a classical physiological discovery, a gut hormone with glucose-dependent insulinotropic action and effects on appetite and gastric emptying, defined in humans, placed in the proglucagon-peptide system, and tied to the truncated active peptide. It has decades of independent confirmation and large randomised outcome trials, including cardiovascular and renal benefit, so maturity is not in question. I also hold that a single part is right. Nobody put forward a second part in round 1, and no second achievement fits within three names without removing one of the GLP-1 physiologists, which would damage the part that carries the clearest discovery.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is disputed, Habener is outside the credited names, and none of us, myself included, can cite primary documents rather than recollection, so the third seat is a judgment about the purpose of the prize and not a finding of fact. Knudsen's acylation work is arguably as decisive for patients as any physiology, and a citation that names the therapies while omitting the person who engineered the long-acting drugs will be criticised. I accept that criticism as real. I think the discovery-focused reading is the more defensible one, but it is a choice and I do not want the citation to present it as self-evident.

responses.point: Sandberg argues that acylation-based half-life extension was a conceptually new scientific step, that Knudsen's contribution is the least disputed in the historical record, and that the Mojsov seat carries more attribution risk because of Habener's group.
responses.response: This is the strongest challenge to my configuration and I have weighed it again. Your point on priority risk is fair: Knudsen's role is cleaner to document than Mojsov's. But a clean record does not settle what the prize is for. Fatty-acid acylation to bind albumin is an ingenious solution to a pharmacokinetic problem, yet it presupposes the identification of the active peptide and the receptor biology, and it is the part of the story most tied to an industrial programme, where credit inside a team is hardest to isolate. I therefore keep Mojsov, while noting that you and I now differ only on that one seat and on the purpose of the prize. I take your point that your own fallback, Mojsov for Knudsen if discovery decides, is consistent with this. I do not see priority risk as a reason to drop her: the disagreement concerns degree of priority for the active form, not whether she identified it.

responses.point: Perlmann would credit Mojsov over Knudsen but wants the citation to name incretin-based therapy explicitly, and says the Mojsov priority question becomes more pressing if development is recognised.
responses.response: I agree with the wording and have kept it: the citation names incretin-based therapy of diabetes and obesity as what the discoveries made possible, which answers the concern that a physiology-only citation ignores the payoff, without crediting drug development. Your condition is also right. If the committee moved Knudsen into the third seat, the citation should say openly that it covers translation, and Mojsov's priority would not need to be settled to the same standard because she would no longer be in the trio. Where I would add a caution is that we should not treat the unresolved priority record as a reason to prefer a seat whose evidence merely looks tidier. I would rather accept an acknowledged judgment on Mojsov than choose by documentary convenience.

responses.point: Linnarsson says that without Eshhar the CAR-T citation becomes narrower than its title, that B014 is the strongest alternative and not a co-equal second part, and that a single-part B049 is preferable.
responses.response: I agree, and the Eshhar point reinforces why I do not pair B014 with B049. A CAR-T citation worded around costimulation and clinical translation for June and Sadelain is defensible but narrower, and Eshhar's absence is an attribution gap that the supplied names cannot close. Combined with GLP-1 it would also force a two-name or one-name GLP-1 part. I keep B014 as my first alternative, for use if the committee cannot defend the GLP-1 trio, and I still would not include Rosenberg, whose adoptive cell therapy is a distinct line.

responses.point: El-Manira now argues that if optogenetics cannot be given a defensible trio without excluding Bamberg, Boyden, Deisseroth or Miesenboeck, that is a reason not to put it at the top this year, and asks whether anyone considers Mojsov's priority settled.
responses.response: On optogenetics I agree with your revised position, and it is why I list B023 and not B021 as my second alternative: the channelrhodopsin discovery and the neuronal demonstration are separate achievements, and any three names exclude someone essential. On your question, I do not consider Mojsov's priority settled, and I do not think any of us can settle it from memory. What I can say is that the dispute concerns degree of priority for the active truncated form, that Holst and Drucker carry the physiology and therapeutic rationale regardless, and that the three of you who would swap in Knudsen only if the committee wants development recognised have described the real fork correctly. I resolve it toward discovery.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius asks for a consistent discovery-versus-development standard across GLP-1, imatinib and CAR-T.
responses.response: I would apply one standard: credit the person or group whose finding defined the biological entity or mechanism that the therapy then exploits, and treat the engineering and clinical optimisation as the consequence, named in the citation but not credited as a laureate seat. On that standard GLP-1 (physiology and active peptide) is a clean fit. Imatinib is an uncomfortable fit because its credited names are clinical and chemical developers of a drug against a target defined by others, and CAR-T is mixed because Eshhar defined the concept while June and Sadelain engineered and tested it. The standard favours Mojsov over Knudsen for B049, but I accept that it also exposes B014 and B011 as weaker on discovery grounds.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should hold the third GLP-1 seat, which turns on the purpose of the prize and on a priority record that none of us can check against primary documents.
Habener's contribution to proglucagon and GLP-1 biology and why he lies outside the credited names; I cannot say how much this should weaken the trio.
Whether the committee will accept a single-part prize or wants a second achievement; I see no configuration that does not damage the GLP-1 attribution.
My recollection of the GLP-1 priority history is unverified against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: No GLP-1, CAR-T, unfolded protein response or optogenetics candidate is connected to me through the provided profile. My documented connections are a postdoctoral period with Paul Greengard, who is not a candidate on this shortlist, and about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy, an unaudited count; neither bears on the shortlisted ballots. No other member reported a conflict with a credited name, and nothing in round 1 changes my disclosure. As chair I am also leading the process.
